articles.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
articles.body_text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

articles.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
articles.body_text: With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3 , the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip. Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades. The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click. Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate. It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach. If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings. The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.) The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149. The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green. Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2 , which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out. The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

articles.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mark Wahlberg, who once sank money into a gym chain that got kicked off the NYSE, is now building his own, and he promises you’ll get a cold plunge, a blood panel and a protein muffin without needing a trust fund.
articles.body_text: Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness. Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing. It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line. The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt. It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.” By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.” Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges . But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.” Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership. Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.” When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand , for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.” He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out). Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “ Wahl Street ,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

articles.title: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery.
articles.body_text: Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling? Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style. My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.) On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful. Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice. The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt . With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to. The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color. There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said. I’d also forgo the illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230). That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such. It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait.

articles.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
articles.body_text: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. articles.title: Waymo's robotaxis are headed to Canada | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The company will start off by testing its self-driving vehicles on Toronto's streets.
articles.body_text: Alphabet’s self-driving car unit, Waymo, is expanding into Canada after receiving approval to participate in Ontario’s automated vehicle pilot program. The company isn’t launching a robotaxi service just yet, though. Waymo tends to follow the same playbook for every new city, gradually proceeding from manual mapping to testing, and eventually operating a commercial service. Waymo said in a blog post on Friday that its self-driving vehicles will be manually driven in Toronto to create high-definition maps of local street networks. The company will then test its autonomous vehicles on public roads with a human safety operator on board. These operators will eventually be pulled from the driver’s seat, and afterwards the company will invite the public to take rides in its robotaxis. Waymo’s move into Canada is part of an aggressive push into new markets that’s picking up speed. Two years ago, the company was operating in only three commercial markets, and its robotaxis were not yet driving on freeways. Its expansion plans kicked off in March 2025 with a deployment in Austin, and later in Atlanta. Today, the company has robotaxi services in 15 U.S. cities, and is testing them in London and Tokyo as well. The company’s co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana said the expansion into Canada marks an important milestone in its global journey. This is also the northernmost and possibly most wintry city that Waymo has so far tried to operate in, so these conditions will test its AV technology and operational savviness. As part of its accelerated expansion strategy, Waymo has started partnering with third-party companies to manage its fleet in each respective city. Toronto is no different: Waymo said it has partnered with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, and expects to support hundreds of jobs in spaces such as fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations. articles.title: In 'You Can See Everything,' Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nathan Fielder's documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has created a constellation of colliding personas that interrogate the very nature of authenticity.
articles.body_text: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes. One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” [The rest of this review contains spoilers.] Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up.

articles.title: Elon Musk tells advertisers: “Go fuck yourself”
articles.summary: Elon Musk said that the X ad boycott could kill his company, but he told advertisers to “stop” instead of trying to “blackmail me.”
articles.body_text: Elon Musk took the stage at the DealBook conference on Wednesday evening with nervous laughter and a cascade of jokes about himself and his companies. But the interview quickly turned to the more serious subject of Musk’s recent antisemitic posts on X (formerly Twitter) and whether his company can survive the advertiser boycott. On that matter, Musk seemed alternatingly apologetic and defiant — acknowledging his mistakes, then doing everything in his power to push advertisers away. “I hope they stop. Don’t advertise,” Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. “If somebody is going to try to blackmail me with advertising, blackmail me with money, go fuck yourself. Go fuck yourself. Is that clear? I hope it is.” He singled out Disney CEO Bob Iger, who discussed not wanting Disney to be affiliated with Musk while onstage earlier in the day. “Hey Bob, if you’re in the audience.” If advertisers don’t return, Musk said, “what this advertising boycott is going to do is it’s going to kill the company.” He seemed almost resigned to the possibility, speaking of it almost as though X were a martyr and advertisers the enemy. “That is what everybody on Earth will know,” he said. “We’ll be gone, and it’ll be gone because of an advertiser boycott.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_M_uvDChJQ] Musk’s message to advertisers came after what had briefly appeared to be an attempt to salvage the damage he caused after he called an antisemitic post the “actual truth” two weeks ago. More than 100 brands have since halted their ads, and the company is at risk of losing $75 million by the end of the year, according to The New York Times. “I should in retrospect should not have replied to that one person,” Musk said. He blamed media outlets for not covering his clarifications before apologizing. “Essentially I handed a loaded gun to those who hate me, and arguably to those are antisemitic, and for that I’m quite sorry. That was not my intention.” But even in his attempts to explain himself — that out of tens of thousands of posts on X, he’s bound to say “foolish” things — Musk insisted he wasn’t on an “apology tour.” He said his recent visit to Israel wasn’t in response to the criticism of his posts and that he didn’t mind being an object of contempt. He then went on a rambling explanation of what he says he really meant: his belief that Jewish people are funding causes meant to “annihilate” them. His attempted clarification only seemed to further the antisemitic conspiracy theory he promoted in the first place, broadly blaming “people in the Jewish community” for their support of unnamed activist groups. X CEO Linda Yaccarino — the former advertising chief at NBCUniversal who Musk brought on board to shore up the platform’s appeal to advertisers — took to X shortly after her CTO’s rant to say this: “Here’s my perspective when it comes to advertising: X is standing at a unique and amazing intersection of Free Speech and Main Street — and the X community is powerful and is here to welcome you. To our partners who believe in our meaningful work — Thank You.” The full interview was meandering and at times devolved into stream of consciousness responses; Musk spoke for triple the time most other interviewees did. But the questions around Musk’s own actions, and the resulting advertiser exodus — the things that could materially impact X — seemed to garner the most nonchalant answers. He doesn’t seem to care. Update November 30th, 4:35AM ET: Added statement from X CEO Linda Yaccarino.

articles.title: Another major ad agency recommends pausing Twitter ad campaigns
articles.summary: Omnicom Media Group recommended that clients (which include Pepsi, Apple, and McDonald’s) pause advertising on Twitter, citing “potential serious implications” since Elon Musk’s takeover. It’s the second of the “big four” agencies to do so, following IPG.
articles.body_text: Omnicom, one of the world’s biggest ad firms, representing brands like McDonald’s, Apple, and PepsiCo, is recommending clients pause spending on Twitter, according to an internal memo obtained by The Verge. Omnicom Media Group is recommending clients “pause activity on Twitter in the short term,” according to a note titled “Twitter - Continued Brand Safety Concerns.” The memo cites recent events in the last few days that have “potential serious implications” for brands running ads on the platform. The memo cites the deep layoffs of Twitter trust and safety teams, the resignations of high-profile executives, and the slew of “verified” impersonation accounts as being key issues for advertisers. There is “evidence that the risk to our clients’ brand safety has risen sharply to a level most would find unacceptable,” the memo reads. “We recommend pausing activity on Twitter in the short term until the platform can prove it has reintroduced safeguards to an acceptable level and has regained control of its environment.” The memo goes on to say that Omnicom has “formally requested that Twitter assure us that these issues will not impact compliant processes, operations, products, brand safety and client investment on the platform in any way” but that “seemingly due to the lack of senior leadership now in these areas, Twitter has not been able to give those assurances.” It’s the latest in a string of advertisers that have changed plans following the chaos at Twitter since Elon Musk’s takeover. Last week, IPG, another ad agency giant, recommended its clients suspend their advertising on Twitter, according to CNBC. Companies like Volkswagen, General Motors, and General Mills have also pulled ad spending from Twitter in recent weeks. The majority of Twitter’s revenue comes from ads, and despite Musk’s questionable efforts at soothing their concerns, advertisers are worried about their content showing up next to an influx of hate speech and impersonations. They’re also concerned about Musk’s own tweets, like his threats to “thermonuclear name & shame” advertisers who pull their money from the platform. In Musk’s first email to Twitter employees, the billionaire owner said roughly half of the company’s revenue would need to come from subscriptions. But in the last few days, Twitter Blue, the premium tier for $7.99 a month that Musk has been pushing, has been through tumultuous changes in the short time it’s been live. As of writing, Twitter Blue has been suspended just days after the rushed launch — though who’s to say that won’t change in an hour.

The moral bankruptcy of Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz
articles.summary: Two of the most famous investors in Silicon Valley endorsed Donald Trump. This is less about tech generally than their investment portfolio, specifically.
articles.body_text: Last week, the founders of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz declared their allegiance to Donald Trump in their customary fashion: talking about money on a podcast. “Sorry, Mom,” Ben Horowitz says in an episode of The Ben & Marc Show. “I know you’re going to be mad at me for this. But, like, we have to do it.” Marc Andreessen and Horowitz insist they voted for Democrats until now. They are friends with liberals. They claim to be nervous about the social blowback they will receive for this, especially because of the historically progressive nature of the tech industry and the Bay Area. But given the general movement among their class toward Trump, I think those claims about being nervous are overblown, if not performative. There is, for instance, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump super PAC, which has support from Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire and 8VC’s Joe Lonsdale, among other notables. (The Wall Street Journal reported Musk is planning to donate $45 million a month, which Musk has denied.) There’s the $160 million the crypto movement has put forward in support of crypto-friendly candidates. We can’t forget their VC pal David Sacks speaking at the Republican National Convention. And last but not least, there’s Trump’s running mate choice of JD Vance, a former venture capitalist whose firm’s investors included Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, and Andreessen himself. This isn’t a movement. It’s a clique. The podcast itself is an extraordinary performance. At one point, Andreessen concedes that their major problems with President Joe Biden — the ones that led them to support Trump — are what most voters would consider “subsidiary” issues. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the big issues that people care about,” he says. If we take this podcast at face value, we are to believe that these subsidiary issues are the only reason they’ve chosen to endorse and donate to Trump. These subsidiary issues take precedence for Andreessen and Horowitz over, say, mass deportations and Project 2025’s attempt to end no-fault divorce. We are looking at a simple trade against personal liberty — abortion, the rights of gay and trans people, and possibly democracy itself — in favor of crypto, AI, and a tax policy they like better. For Horowitz, “probably the most emotional topic” is crypto — a16z started a $4.5 billion crypto fund in 2022, and the pair believe that the Biden administration has been deeply unfair to crypto. In Horowitz’s view, the Biden administration “basically subverted the rule of law to attack the crypto industry.” Certainly much of the crypto industry prefers Trump. But it seems obvious that there has been a lot of intra-agency squabbling as Congress dithered on passing any laws. To place the blame squarely on Biden is bizarre, particularly when we have Trump’s chaotic previous term as guidance. Sure, Trump is no longer saying Bitcoin is “a scam against the dollar,” as he did in 2021; he is scheduled to speak at the Bitcoin conference this year. But his record in office is not exactly pro-crypto. During the Trump administration, financial regulator FinCEN initially asked the public to provide comments on a crypto rule change over a 15-day period that included Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day, which effectively shortened the comment window by four working days. There is also the Ripple Labs enforcement case, in which the SEC is seeking a $1.95 billion fine; it, too, dates to the Trump administration. The pair’s complaints about Gary Gensler, the current head of the Securities and Exchange Commission, are striking. They are particularly annoyed that he won’t pay attention to them. “We’re the largest crypto investors or largest blockchain investors in the world, and we’ve requested meetings with him at least a half a dozen times,” Horowitz says. Gensler has not met with them. Neither, they say, has Senator Elizabeth Warren or Biden himself. In fact, Andreessen makes it clear that he expects presidential attention, something he’s been getting since he was 23. Given the number of times Andreessen and Horowitz make references to various meetings with various politicians, it’s easy to get the impression that they are mostly insulted that they are being treated like ordinary constituents. From crypto, we move to AI, which Andreessen and Horowitz don’t think is being regulated correctly either. According to Horowitz, AI is as powerful as, or more powerful than, the internet and the global computer industry from the 1950s on. “This may be the biggest technological boom of all time,” Andreessen says. Andreessen says in his newsletter-cum-manifesto, “The Little Tech Agenda,” that he is worried that AI will face similar scrutiny to crypto. The FTC has issued guidance to the AI industry that indicated it will pursue companies that exaggerate what their AI can do, say they are using AI when they are not, and recklessly put products on the market without properly analyzing the risks. Meanwhile, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has told lenders that they must supply a reason for a credit denial that’s better than just “computer says no” when using AI models. These regulations have little to do with technology and a lot to do with old-fashioned lying. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz single out Biden’s executive order about artificial intelligence. The order requires companies to disclose the presence of very large models, as well as to provide the government information about what the plans are for the model, what cybersecurity measures are taken to protect those models, and the results of red-team testing for sensitive subjects, among other things. This is in keeping with Horowitz’s assertion about the seriousness of the technology. So what’s the problem? The two focus on computing power. The disclosure requirements apply to “any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations.” Andreessen and Horowitz think specifying such a limit is ridiculous. Little tech “will be snuffed out by this kind of regulation,” Horowitz says. It is perhaps worth noting that nothing above the size specified in the executive order — the size Andreessen and Horowitz object to — even exists yet, according to Arati Prabhakar, Biden’s top tech advisor. The fundamental complaint here is that these two believe that the Biden administration’s approach to AI “enshrine[s] the two or three companies that they believe are the only companies that matter as sort of permanent monopolies,” Andreessen says. “And they’re going to just basically destroy the startup ecosystem underneath that.” Andreessen Horowitz is, of course, invested in that ecosystem, having earmarked $2.25 billion for AI applications and infrastructure. The anti-monopoly rhetoric is in keeping with a16z’s latest marketing push. According to Andreessen’s newsletter, startups are threatened by the government, which is “now far more hostile to new startups than it used to be.” Besides his objections to the way the SEC has increased its oversight of crypto, he is also upset that a stepped-up interest in antitrust has made it more difficult for him to exit investments. “Regulatory agencies are punitively blocking startups from being acquired by the same big companies the government is preferencing in so many other ways,” Andreessen writes. After all, the Federal Trade Commission has launched an inquiry into Big Tech’s partnerships and investments with startups — with the goal of seeing if those partnerships squash competition. The irony is so obvious it’s almost embarrassing to point it out. Andreessen says he is upset that Big Tech is too powerful, but he opposes antitrust action because that blocks a route for VCs to exit. Either you’re comfortable with Big Tech getting bigger, in which case acquisitions are fine, or you want little tech to be competitive, which means blocking industry consolidation. Mainly, it seems that Andreessen believes in cashing out. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz pointedly name Google as a threat to startups. “Google, I think we would all agree, is more powerful than probably 95 percent of countries in the world,” Horowitz says at one point. Google, specifically, is a sore spot with the right wing. Vice presidential nominee Vance has already said it should be broken up. Vance believes Google is controlling information and skewing too far left. Of course, Google’s moderation policies don’t just apply to Google News — they also affect YouTube, which hosts a great many right-wing podcasts without issue. It’s unclear how seriously to take Andreessen and Horowitz’s complaints about Big Tech because the complaints don’t quite square with their behavior. For instance, Facebook is similarly powerful and influential, especially in AI. Andreessen sits on its board. A16z is invested in OpenAI, which has a partnership with Microsoft — and both have lobbied strenuously for more regulation around AI. It sure seems like if a16z wants to change things at those big companies, someone could simply pick up the phone. At this point in the podcast, you could squint and say maybe the concern about AI and crypto is really about technology and progress. But from those two topics, we move on to classic rich guy shit of the most tedious kind: tax reform. Andreessen says it was “the final straw for me. This is the thing that tipped me hard.” They are upset about a proposal to alter capital gains taxes. Capital gains are paid on investment assets, and they are typically paid when the investment is sold and the gains are, in industry terms, “realized.” The new Biden treasury proposal means that for people whose wealth is worth more than $100 million, any unrealized capital gains will be taxed, too. This is what has Andreessen and Horowitz in a tizzy. It means that if they own a clutch of highly valued startup shares, they will have to pay taxes on them before they cash out. This is a “very scary proposal,” Horowitz says. Startups are illiquid assets, Andreessen points out. “Startups never go up and down. They’re never overvalued,” says Horowtiz, dryly. “There’s no bubbles.” Andreessen notes that the way the value of a startup is calculated for the purposes of this proposed tax has to do with the latest round’s valuation. Historically, one of the ways that Andreessen Horowitz has approached startup investing is to inflate a company’s valuation; it is “the OG when it comes to doling out speculative startup valuations.” The new proposed tax punishes this kind of behavior — a high valuation means a high tax. “This makes startups completely implausible,” says Andreessen. “Venture capital just ends. Firms like ours don’t exist.” This is followed by an anxiety spiral that is sort of difficult to convey in text; I suggest you listen for yourself. “California is done,” says Andreessen. “It’s total destruction.” The taxes won’t just target the wealthy; they’ll come for everyone. “Once the structure gets established, the politicians do what they do: they’ll walk the numbers up,” Andreessen says. “Presto chango, we’re Argentina!” says Horowitz. Finally, Horowitz gets ahold of himself. “By the way, this one probably won’t get all the way through the system,” he says. “But it might!” There is another issue that might cause wreckage throughout Silicon Valley. It is immigration. An awful lot of immigrants comprise Silicon Valley’s talent pool — a huge swath of engineers in the US are on H-1B visas. The Trump / Vance ticket is virulently anti-immigrant. The current CEOs of Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are all immigrants. So are Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates are involved in Fwd.us, a lobbying group dedicated to immigration reform that Musk and Sacks both left. If there were an issue that would rally the people who care most about progress, innovation, and talent, you’d think protecting the immigrants who’ve built lives and careers in tech would be it. Stopping immigration is a core issue of the Trump campaign. During the Republican National Convention, delegates held up signs saying “Mass Deportation Now.” Trump has called the H-1B, the visa many tech workers use to come to Silicon Valley, “very bad” and “unfair” to US workers. In his previous term, he targeted H-1B visa applications specifically; in the fiscal year 2018, almost 25 percent of applications were denied, up from about 13 percent the year before. In fiscal year 2019, 20 percent of H-1B applications were denied. The denials plummeted after several Trump administration rules were thrown out by courts; the denial rate in 2022 was just 2 percent. Immigration plainly matters for crypto — as Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin says, “The crypto industry is uniquely international, and so immigration law is crypto law.” Buterin is one of the most influential voices in crypto, and Ethereum is the foundation for a swath of Andreessen Horowitz’s investment portfolio. Among the investments that rely on it are MakerDAO, VeeFriends, Dapper Labs, and EigenLayer. It is remarkable that the founder of Ethereum is saying that voting for Trump is against the crypto ethos, and the big crypto investors are doing it anyway. The word “immigration” is only mentioned by Andreessen and Horowitz in the podcast when they discuss the rally in which someone attempted an assassination: Trump had turned his head to look at a chart that purported to show illegal immigration into the US as the bullet whizzed by. I wondered why such an important issue for tech wasn’t addressed, so I emailed Margit Wennmachers, a16z’s PR guru, to ask. She didn’t reply. After I finished listening to the podcast, a few things kept nagging at me. Take the very beginning of the podcast. Once upon a time, Andreessen says, you could get very rich and then give the money away in philanthropy, “and you get enormous credit for that. And, you know, it absolves you of whatever.” At some point in the last 10 years, some people suggested that maybe rich people should pay more taxes instead of giving their money away — that perhaps the whims of some random rich person are not the best way to support the most vulnerable in our society. Andreessen and Horowitz suggest that this critique of philanthropy is simply jealousy. It also unbalanced “the deal.” “The deal,” as described on the podcast, is vague. To my ear, it sounds like this: Tech companies could basically do whatever they wanted, as long as people who worked there paid high taxes and donated enough money to charitable causes. The money — taxes, donations — made them the good guys. Andreessen and Horowitz point to the mid-2010s — that is, the era of low interest rates — as the time of “the deal” unraveling. Notably, this is around the time that the tech hype cycle became obvious even to people who weren’t paying attention. This year, it’s scooters! Now it’s viral media companies! Now it’s metaverse! Now it’s crypto! Now it’s AI! These ideas were more or less rejected by the market, except possibly AI. The one thing all these hype cycles had in common was VCs talking their books, as publicly as possible. That charge was led by Andreessen Horowitz. So now, instead of investing in things the market wants, Andreessen and Horowitz appear to be gambling on legislation instead. Their timing is remarkable; not even a week after their Trump endorsement, Biden dropped out of the race, rallying the Democrats behind Vice President Kamala Harris. In the hours immediately following the announcement, small-money donors raised $46.7 million for her campaign. By endorsing Trump, Andreessen and Horowitz have effectively lost whatever leverage they might have had with the Harris campaign. But maybe that doesn’t matter. Near the end of the podcast, Horowitz says that he was shaken by the assassination attempt on Donald Trump because he’s friends with Ivanka, his daughter, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. “Ivanka and the kids were just at my house,” Horowitz says, of learning Trump was shot. “We went to see David Copperfield and all that. So my brain was almost frozen because I had this feeling about, ‘Oh my god, Grandpa just got shot.’” As for Andreessen, he has been inveighing against “woke” capital, engaging in Twitter culture wars, and complaining about what he views as the media’s hostility to free speech for a while now. In Andreessen’s 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” he lists what he terms “patron saints” of the movement. They include Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian futurist who was also the co-author of The Fascist Manifesto; Nick Land, whose writing is a foundational text for the so-called alt-right; Neven Sesardic, a philosopher who argues that race is biologically real and not socially constructed; and Vilfredo Pareto, who argued that democracy is an illusion. And this talk about democracy brings me to Curtis Yarvin, personal friend of vice presidential candidate Vance. Yarvin, a software developer, is openly anti-democracy. (Yarvin’s recent newsletter, in response to Biden dropping out, enthusiastically advocates for a return to monarchy. Freak shit.) One of Yarvin’s ideas, called “retire all government employees” or RAGE, is part of Project 2025, a Heritage Foundation proposal for what Trump should do if he wins. This rhetoric was echoed by Vance in 2021, who called out Yarvin by name. So this VC cabal is trading against the basic principles of America — not merely against personal freedom, but democracy itself — in the hopes of profit. It’s not the first time tech has made the trade against freedom; IBM made it during the Holocaust. In venture capital, you are what you fund. Andreessen and Horowitz understand this, even embody it. But they aren’t just funding the issues they discuss on their podcast; they are funding Trump and Vance. That means those donations are anti-abortion, anti-immigration, and possibly even anti-democracy because that is what the Trump / Vance ticket stands for. These are not subsidiary issues: these are now what two of Silicon Valley’s most prominent figures now stand for, too. Is that a good investment? Correction July 24: An earlier version of this article misstated the donation strategy of a crypto super PAC. The group also spends money on Democratic candidates, not just right-wing ones.

articles.title: ”Det vidrigaste jag har gjort”
articles.summary: Jonas ”Heavy” Stentäpp var en stor profil i folkrace-Sverige. I ett känslosamt tal hyllas han nu av vännen Michael Hjelm.
articles.body_text: Jonas ”Heavy” Stentäpp var en stor profil i folkrace-Sverige. I ett känslosamt tal hyllas han nu av vännen Michael Hjelm. ”Det var det vidrigaste jag gjort, men också det finaste”‚ skriver Hjelm till Expressen. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Jonas ”Heavy” Stentäpp gick bort tidigare i veckan i sviterna efter den lungcancer han drabbades av i somras. Som ena halvan av duon ”Hjalle och Heavy” blev han känd för svenska folket när de medverkade i TV4-succén ”På rymmen” i slutet av 1990-talet. Men ”Heavy” hade också ett stort engagemang för folkrace och var med och byggde upp sajten Folkracepuls, som han fram till sin död var chefredaktör för. I helgen var det final i Skaraborgscupen i Ulricehamn. Då höll folkrace-speakern Michael Hjelm tal där han hedrade sin nära vän. Där berättade han om när de båda lärde känna varandra, och att ”Heavy” som även var musiker skrev en låt till Michael Hjelm. – Efter den dagen har vi kamperat ihop, med jävligt knasiga idéer och påhitt. Och det gör bara så jävla ont, säger Michael Hjelm innan rösten bryts. Han berättar också om sin saknad och leder de närvarande i en tyst minut. – Vi ställer oss upp, och behåller kepsen på! Den ska vara på för dig, ”Heavy”, säger Michael Hjelm.

articles.title: Därför kan Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist (C) få sondera • ”Mycket möjligt”
articles.summary: Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist (C) vill fortfarande se en regering ”i mitten av svensk politik”. Att ge henne sonderingsuppdraget framöver kanske skulle bidra till att luckra upp låsningar, tror experter. – Det är mycket möjligt att hon får det, säger Malin Lernfelt, chefredaktör för Liberala nyhetsbyrån.
articles.body_text: Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist (C) vill fortfarande se en regering ”i mitten av svensk politik”. Att ge henne sonderingsuppdraget framöver kanske skulle bidra till att luckra upp låsningar, tror experter. – Det är mycket möjligt att hon får det, säger Malin Lernfelt, chefredaktör för Liberala nyhetsbyrån. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Centerpartiet vill att nästa regering ska vara förankrad i mitten av svensk politik och flera partiföreträdare har efter valet sagt att svenska folket ”inte har röstat för en vänstersväng”. Enligt C-källor för man samtal med både Kristdemokraterna och Moderaterna. Centerpartiet nobbar dessutom gemensamma rödgröna möten i riksdagen. Vänsterpartiet tycker att Centerledaren Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist borde få sonderingsuppdraget av talmannen, så att partiet sedan ska välja sida. – Jag tycker det är rimligt att Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, som fortsätter prata om andra regeringskonstellationer, får möjlighet att utreda dem och får en slutpunkt i dem, sa V-ledaren Nooshi Dadgostar häromdagen. Malin Lernfelt, chefredaktör för Liberala nyhetsbyrån, tror att Thand Ringqvist kan få sonderingsuppdraget efter att Moderatledaren Ulf Kristersson fått det och misslyckats. – Eftersom situationen är så låst som den är, och ur ett demokratiskt perspektiv för att försöka luckra upp låsningarna, kan jag tänka mig att talmannen – efter att Kristersson fått det, försökt och gett upp – kanske ger det till Thand Ringqvist, eftersom hon fortfarande pratar om den mittenvision hon har, säger hon och fortsätter: – Sedan kommer det inte att gå. Men för att hon ”ska få känna på det” är det mycket möjligt att hon får det. Malin Lernfelt tror dock inte att C-ledarens sonderingsuppdrag skulle förenas med en statsministeromröstning.

articles.summary: Mannen tog strypgrepp på sin sambo och pressade hennes ansikte mot en kudde så att hon fick andnöd. Dagen innan hade skärpta regler om utvisning på grund av brott börjat gälla. Nu utvisas mannen, som bott i Sverige sedan fem års ålder. – Ribban för utvisning är lägre nu, säger Anders Larsson, chefsrådman vid Södertörns tingsrätt.
articles.body_text: Mannen tog strypgrepp på sin sambo och pressade hennes ansikte mot en kudde så att hon fick andnöd. Dagen innan hade skärpta regler om utvisning på grund av brott börjat gälla. Nu utvisas mannen, som bott i Sverige sedan fem års ålder. – Ribban för utvisning är lägre nu, säger Anders Larsson, chefsrådman vid Södertörns tingsrätt. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Mannen och kvinnan hade varit och grillat men blivit osams vilket ledde till att de tog bussen hem till den gemensamma lägenheten söder om Stockholm. På väg in i lägenheten eskalerade situationen. Mannen tog ett strypgrepp med armen runt kvinnans hals och pressade därefter hennes ansikte mot en kudde så att hon fick kraftig andnöd och drabbades av panik. Kvinnan orsakades blåmärken, underhudsblödningar, blödning i ögongloben, svullnad, hudavskrapning och smärta. Den 30-årige mannen dömdes förra veckan till fängelse i ett år och tre månader för misshandel. Han är medborgare i Polen, och åklagaren begärde honom utvisad. Mannen har bott i Sverige sedan han var fem år. Efter ett avgörande i Hösta domstolen våren 2025 har domstolarna varit mycket restriktiva med att utvisa utländska medborgare som kommit till Sverige som barn. Det fallet gällde en chilensk medborgare som dömts till fyra års fängelse för bland annat grovt vapenbrott, grovt olaga hot och övergrepp i rättssak. Hovrätten hade utvisat honom med tio års återreseförbud. Högsta domstolen, som instämde i att risken för fortsatt brottslighet var hög, tog dock fasta på att mannen kommit till Sverige som spädbarn och lät honom stanna. Sedan dess har dock lagen ändrats. I juni i år antog riksdagen Tidöregeringens proposition om skärpta regler om utvisning på grund av brott. Lagändringens uttalade syfte är att fler brottslingar ska utvisas, och migrationsminister Johan Forssell har talat om att det kan bli en sexdubbling av antalet brottsutvisningar.

articles.title: Trumps utbrott: ”Förstört landet”
articles.summary: Våldsamma demonstrationer skakade Frankrike under lördagen. Plundringar, bränder och upplopp skakade stora delar av landet. Nu kallar premiärministern till krismöte, enligt Le Figaro.
articles.body_text: Plundringar, bränder och upplopp skakade stora delar av landet. Nu kallar premiärministern till krismöte, enligt Le Figaro . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. I går bröt kaos ut i flera av Frankrikes största städer. I dag visar bilder gator som ser ut som ödesmarker efter plundringar, upplopp och uppbrända bilar. I Limoges har stadshuset brunnit ner. Över 1 800 demonstranter har gripits och utredningar pågår för att hitta fler förövare, skriver Frankrikes inrikesminister Laurent Nuñez på X . Samtidigt skadades över 500 poliser, brandmän och medlemmar i säkerhetsstyrkan. Frankrikes premiärminister Sébastien Lecornu har kallat till krismöte mellan ministerierna klockan 18 på söndagen, enligt Le Figaro. President Emmanuel Macron kommer att delta på mötet – och sedan hålla tal till nationen klockan 20. Både Macron och Lecornu fördömde protesterna under gårdagen. Under söndagen delar även USA:s president Donald Trump sin syn på upploppen. ”Frankrike brinner!” skriver han i ett inlägg på Truth Social. Enligt honom har invandringen ”förstört det en gång så fantastiska landet”. Han uppmanar Frankrike till att stänga gränserna.

articles.title: Jysk stänger
articles.summary: Den 8 november håller Jysk stängt i hela Sverige när 1 500 medarbetare samlas för den årliga personalfesten i Göteborg.
articles.body_text: Den 8 november håller alla landets 160 butiker stängt. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. På söndag den 8 november slår samtliga Jyskbutiker i Sverige igen. Medarbetarna ska på fest. Möbeljätten håller nämligen sin årliga personalfest kvällen innan. I år hålls den i Göteborg. – Vi vill att så många som möjligt ska kunna delta på festen och kunna ta sig hem i lugn och ro. Det är en bit resväg för en del av medarbetarna, vi har butiker från Kiruna till Trelleborg, säger Sandra Martinsson, kommunikationschef på Jysk Sverige. På lördagen har det satts in vikarier i flera av landets butiker så att de fastanställda ska kunna resa till Göteborg. 1 500 medarbetare har anmält sig, vilket gör årets fest till den största hittills. Jysk stänger sina butiker varje år i samband med festen. Än så länge har de inte fått så många negativa kommentarer av kunder, berättar Martinsson. – Vi fick in ett klagomål förra året när en kund hade åkt till en butik som visade sig vara stängd. Det löste vi i efterhand, men det blev en lärdom. I år ska vi vara ännu tydligare, både med skyltning och digital information, så att ingen åker dit i onödan och möts av stängda dörrar, säger hon. Festen kostar runt tio miljoner kronor. Och enligt Martinsson innebär stängningen såklart en omsättningsförlust. – Men vad försäljningsbortfallet är har vi faktiskt inte räknat på, vår vd Johan Sjödin har sagt att det inte spelar någon roll. Vi ska stänga den dagen ändå, det är bara så kulturen är, säger hon. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. Expressen granskar, avslöjar och ger dig senaste nyheterna på ett sakligt sätt. Mer om oss här. articles.title: Satellitens rörelser oroar experterna
articles.summary: En rysk satellit har gjort en mystisk manöver som väcker oro bland experter. På bara ett dygn har den minskat avståndet till en amerikansk satellit med över 30 mil – och befinner sig nu knappt fem kilometer bort.
articles.body_text: En rysk satellit har gjort en mystisk manöver som väcker oro bland experter. På bara ett dygn har den minskat avståndet till en amerikansk satellit med över 30 mil – och befinner sig nu knappt fem kilometer bort. – Det är i praktiken stötfångare mot stötfångare, säger rymdforskaren Clayton Swope till Axios . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Det handlar om den ryska satelliten Cosmos 2612 och den amerikanskägda ICEYE-X36. Enligt rymdövervakningsföretaget LeoLabs befann sig satelliterna drygt 30 mil från varandra på torsdagen. Ett dygn senare hade avståndet krymp till omkring 4,8 kilometer. I ett uttalande på fredagen uppgav LeoLabs att satellitens rörelser tyder på att Ryssland medvetet försökt närma sig den amerikanska och konstaterade att beteendet ”motiverar fortsatt övervakning”. Manövern beskrevs som ”relativt ovanlig” i den låga omloppsbanan runt jorden, där satelliter kan färdas i hastigheter på över 27 000 kilometer i timmen. Greg Gillinger, rymdanalytiker vid Integrity ISR, delar bedömningen att rörelserna tyder på ett medvetet agerande. – Allt detta är ovanligt och pekar helt enkelt på en avsiktlig interaktion mellan Ryssland och en väststyrd satellit som stöder Ukraina, säger han till Axios. Satelliten ICEYE-X36 tillhör ett nätverk som drivs av det finskgrundade företaget ICEYE, vars teknik används av Ukrainas försvarsmakt. I januari meddelade företaget att samarbetet mellan parterna skulle utökas för att stärka landets satellitbaserade underrättelseförmåga.

articles.title: Sörjer mördade kvinnan: ”Fin tjej”
articles.summary: En kvinna i 25-årsåldern sköts till döds i Kämpetorpshallen i Älvsjö. Nu sörjs hon av kolleger och Hammarby fotboll, som kommer att spela i sorgband.
articles.body_text: Sorgen efter att en kvinna sköts ihjäl i Älvsjö är stor. Utanför idrottshallen där hon mördades har en minnesplats växt fram. – Det är fortfarande svårt att förstå, säger en 12-årig flicka som kände kvinnan. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ljus och blombuketter har ställts utanför Kämpetorpshallen i Älvsjö på söndagsförmiddagen. Det var härifrån larmet kom några minuter efter klockan 21 i fredagskväll. En kvinna i 25-årsåldern hade blivit skjuten, mitt under pågående idrottsevenemang där många barn och unga närvarade. Hon fördes till sjukhus med allvarliga skador. Ett dygn senare meddelade polisen att kvinnans liv inte gått att rädda. – Det är en fruktansvärd tragedi. Våra tankar går givetvis till de nära och kära, säger Lee Orberson, stadsdelsdirektör i Hägersten-Älvsjö, där kvinnan var anställd. Han beskriver kvinnan som en mycket omtyckt och uppskattad kollega. Hennes död berör hela personalgruppen djupt, säger han. Men även barn och unga påverkas av dödsbeskedet. Den mördade kvinnan var välkänd bland unga i området, berättar Orberson. – Hon hade en positiv inverkan på så många, säger han. Många som kände kvinnan har tagit sig till minnesplatsen utanför Kämpetorpshallen. En av dem är en 12-årig flicka, som bland annat brukade träffa kvinnan på ungdomsgården.

articles.title: Ministerns ord efter avslöjandet
articles.summary: Expressens granskning av Lily Abdelshahed sätter press på regeringen i debatten om könstillhörighetslagen, enligt Ekots rapportering.
articles.body_text: Expressen har kunnat berätta om oro och rädsla på Ystads kvinnoanstalt efter att barnamördaren Lily Abdelshahed placerats där. Nu kommenterar socialtjänstministern fallet. – Det biologiska könet ska vara styrande i fler situationer, säger Camilla Waltersson Grönvall (M) till Ekot . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Förra veckan publicerade Expressen en granskning om livstidsdömda Lily Abdelshahed, tidigare Paulus Abdelshahed, som flyttats till kvinnoanstalten i Ystad efter att ha bytt juridiskt kön. Flera intagna vittnar om sexuella kränkningar och otrygghet kopplat till placeringen – då Abdelshahed bland annat går runt och ”visar snoppen”. Granskningen har lett till reaktioner från politiskt håll . Exempelvis har Sverigedemokraterna sagt att det är för lätt att byta kön – medan Miljöpartiet anser ansvaret ligger hos Kriminalvården, då problemet ”inte har med könstillhörighetslagen att göra”. Den nya könstillhörighetslagen trädde i kraft 1 juli 2025. I januari i år meddelade Moderaterna att lagen ska ses över. Utredningen har ännu inte presenterats. Nu har Abdelshaheds fall satt press på partiet, rapporterar Ekot. På torsdag har Rickard Jermsten, Kriminalvårdens generaldirektör, kallats till riksdagens justitieutskott. – Moderaterna vill ha en utredning som går ”ännu längre”. Det biologiska könet ska vara styrande i fler situationer, säger socialtjänstminister Camilla Waltersson Grönvall (M) i en kommentar till radion. Vid årsskiftet väntas även en utredning av fängelselagen presenteras.
